newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Mercy flights privatised as governments step back.
newsitem.headline: Mercy flights privatised as governments step back.

text.p: A private mercy flight evacuated 240 people from Phnom Penh on Wednesday, highlighting how the business sector is providing services that have become too risky or expensive for governments to deliver.

More than 500 hundred people of various nationalities, including many children, were milling alongside the tarmac at Pochentong airport as a Lockheed L1011 passenger plane with 295 seats landed late on Wednesday afternoon.
It was the first non-military flight in or out of the Cambodian capital since two days of heavy fighting at the weekend virtually shut the country down.
Thai, Philippine, Singaporean and Malaysian military aircraft began landing on Tuesday to evacuate their nationals. Others were allowed out on a 'space-available' basis.
That left a number of people, including Westerners employed by major companies inside Cambodia, with no way out.
International SOS Assistance flew to the rescue. The firm, headquartered in Geneva, provides medical and security evacuation by land, sea and air.

"Ministries of Foreign Affairs and State Departments used to do this work, but there have been cuts and retrenchments and we are helping to fill the gap," said Dennis Sullivan, who supervised the SOS evacuation on Wednesday.

"What we're doing in Cambodia is pulling out clients from what has become a civil war-type situation. This is a big operation. but we're experienced. We've done this in Albania, Algeria, Yemen and a few places in Africa."
Sullivan, manager of Security Services for SOS, spent 13 years as a U.S. Navy intelligence officer.
He now puts his analytical skills to work analysing the risks to clients in hot spots around the world and evaluating when and how to mount evacuations.
"We are obligated to our clients to make a 'best effort' to get them out, and today's flight is certainly one of those 'best efforts'," Sullivan said.
"We only go in when it's safe and legal. This is not like the Ross Perot evacuation in Tehran in 1981. We're not armed."

Sullivan refused to disclose the names of the companies he was servicing in Cambodia. Some purchase evacuation insurance at $250 per person annually and others pay a company premium plus actual evacuation costs.

Reporters on the ground were able to identify employees and their dependants from British American Tobacco, Tiger Beer and Bates Advertising boarding the Lockheed aircraft, which flew to and from Bangkok.
Also boarding were some individuals who had to pay what was rumoured to be $1,500 each to get out.
"Don't ask me how I feel about leaving unless you have about $5,000 to give me," said one American woman, who refused to give her name, boarding with two family members.
"I thought this was why I paid taxes, so I could count on my government to get me out of a scrape like this."

A number of Americans arriving in Bangkok from Phnom Penh on Thai military flights on Tuesday said they were unhappy about what they saw as the U.S. government's lack of timely assistance in trying to escape Cambodia.
